🔹 Shana Tova 🔹 Fiji's embassy in Jerusalem 🔹 Lacrosse team wins Europe 🔹 9th best hospital in the world 🔹 A new spy satellite 🔹

Special Middle East Report / 🌸 Good News 🌸 / Wednesday, September 24

“Next year in a rebuilt Jerusalem.” 
For thousands of years of exile, the Jewish people marked Rosh Hashanah with prayers to return home—year after year, through pogroms and wars. And now, 2,000 years later, we are here again: Jerusalem is built, growing, and thriving as the capital of a strong and independent Israel. A tiny country, surrounded by enemies, yet the world’s 26th largest economy (nominally!) —with just 10 million people. A hub of high-tech, bursting with life, young, energetic, with many children—no longer willing to be bent or beaten down.

There is no better time than Rosh Hashanah for a roundup of good news, a reminder that Israel is so much more than what the world wants to see in it, the bad side in an endless conflict. The Jewish people are at their highest point in history, and on track to reach new peaks. Shana Tova to you and your families - may the new year be filled with great news, prosperity, happiness, good health and sense of satisfaction.

🔹 Manor Solomon, Spanish Villarreal’s new signing, came off the bench in the 94th minute to score his first goal in yellow—securing a dramatic victory over Sevilla. The home crowd greeted his entrance with boos; he silenced them with a goal.

🔹 Nearly four in five Greeks support strengthening military, economic, and energy ties with Israel. While Europe’s political leaders often bend to Islamist pressures, ordinary Europeans largely stand with Israel.

A new survey in Greece shows overwhelming support for deepening relations with Israel, despite left-wing demands to downgrade ties in response to the Gaza war. Much like in Britain and elsewhere, most reasonable people recoil at the alliance between the far-left and political Islam. Many recognize that Israel is fighting their war. Greece, in particular, relies heavily on its partnership with Israel in its quiet struggle against Turkey.

🔹 In early September, Israel launched its Ofek-19 reconnaissance satellite. Israel is one of only a handful of nations—between three and five worldwide—capable of building a spy satellite, mounting it on an indigenous rocket, and launching it into orbit. Israel is also the only country that launches satellites against the Earth’s rotation, to ensure that in case of failure they do not crash into hostile Arab states, which only makes this achievement even bigger.

Ofek-19 can capture images of objects smaller than 50 centimeters and transmit photos directly to forces on the ground. For Israel, eyes in the sky are essential, with enemies stretching thousands of kilometers away—from Iran to the Houthis in Yemen to Greta Thunberg’s flotilla.

🔹 Asia Times reports that Israel is selling arms to the Philippines and training local security forces in counterterrorism tactics. A former Spanish colony named after King Felipe II, the Philippines gained independence (for the second time) in 1946 after World War II. Israeli exports to the nation—17 times Israel’s size—peaked at $340 million in 2022.

🔹 Fiji has become the seventh country to open its embassy in Jerusalem, following the United States, Guatemala, Kosovo, Honduras, Paraguay, and Papua New Guinea. Other nations, including Argentina, Hungary, and the Czech Republic, have pledged to follow suit but have yet to act.

🔹 Two Israeli marathoners finished in the top 10 at the World Athletics Championship in Tokyo (Sept. 15). Haimro Alame placed fourth with a time of 2:10:03, just 10 seconds behind Tanzania’s Alphonce Simbu. Gashau Ayale came seventh with 2:10:27.

🔹 Newsweek has ranked Israel’s Sheba Medical Center among the world’s smartest hospitals for 2026, placing it ninth globally—up one spot from last year. This marks the fifth consecutive year Sheba has appeared on the elite list, and it remains Israel’s sole entry. The ranking recognizes innovation, advanced technologies, and digital medicine—placing Sheba alongside the world’s medical giants in the U.S., Europe, and Asia.

🔹 Which universities produce the most startup founders? Despite Israel’s size—just 3% of the U.S.—two Israeli institutions made the global top 20: Tel Aviv University (7th) and the Technion (16th). Aside from one Indian entry at 19th, all other schools are American. Not bad.

🔹 Israel has reopened an embassy in Zambia, after a 52-year absence. The Christian-majority nation of 21 million, 34 times Israel’s size, lies between southern and central Africa. Israel is strengthening its ties in Africa that in turn will help it in the global arena. Zambia's voice in the UN is equal to France's. 

🔹 A world first, in Israel: a spinal cord transplant in a human patient— a potential breakthrough that could restore mobility to the paralyzed. Tel Aviv University announced that the surgery, planned for the coming months, marks a milestone in regenerative medicine.

Led by Prof. Tal Dvir and biotech firm Matricelf, the project follows 2022 lab success in growing a human spinal cord and implanting it into paralyzed animal models—results hailed in the journal Advanced Science.

🔹 Passenger traffic at Ben Gurion Airport is back to pre-October 7 levels. On August 21, more than 89,000 travelers passed through on 513 international flights. Since then, the numbers have only risen, boosted by the gradual return of foreign airlines. Carriers from Europe and Asia have resumed operations, expanding both business and tourist routes. Delta Airlines and AirBaltic are expected to return soon, while Wizz Air is ramping up service—driving numbers even higher.

In a single day, more people leave Israel than Gazans leave Gaza in an entire year. That’s what a modern, democratic, first-world nation looks like—versus a failed enclave at perpetual war with its neighbor.

🔹 Speaking of Wizz Air: Israel’s Transportation Ministry is working to establish a local hub for the budget airline, which recently resumed flights to Israel. Such a base would reduce costs, lower ticket prices, and position Israel as a major transfer hub between Europe, Asia, and Africa. Plans include a hangar, crew facilities, and even the possibility of domestic flights—such as to Eilat. CEO József Váradi is expected to visit Israel soon to advance the deal.

🔹 Staying in aviation: A direct route between Tel Aviv and Hanoi will launch in January 2026.

🔹 In July, Israel’s national lacrosse team won the European Championship, edging Italy 9–8. Remarkably, it was only the team’s third-ever tournament. With lacrosse set to join the Olympic Games in Los Angeles 2028, the blue-and-white may soon find themselves competing on the world’s biggest stage.

🔹 90% of the residents of northern Israel and 90% of the residents if the communities near Gaza have returned to their homes. The residents who lived along the borders were forced to leave their homes, live far from their communities, and give up so much for nearly two years. But now they are closing the circle and returning to the path of rebuilding. This is the Jewish story, this is the Israeli story: you cannot defeat a people that chooses life over everything else, time and again 🙏🇮🇱💪

More pictures below 😀

Nearly 2 million people have been evacuated in southern China as Typhoon Ragasa, one of the strongest storms of the year, makes landfall along the densely populated coastline.
The powerful storm brought Hong Kong and large parts of southern China to a standstill on Wednesday, after sweeping through the Philippines and Taiwan with destructive force. Ragasa, packing hurricane-strength winds, triggered landslides, flooding, and massive waves, and is now battering Guangdong province, home to major cities such as Shenzhen and Guangzhou.
In Taiwan, at least 17 people have been confirmed dead, while 17 more remain missing after a natural dam collapsed on Tuesday, unleashing some 68 million tons of water that inundated Guangfu township. Rescuers continue efforts to locate the missing as the storm’s devastation unfolds.

data.text:
$BABA Alibaba’s Apsara announcements are strategically significant because they reset the company’s center of gravity toward AI-first infrastructure and software, while leveraging external and internal compute options to de-risk U.S. export controls and revive Alibaba Cloud’s growth and monetization narrative. The company unveiled Qwen3‑Max, a >1 trillion-parameter flagship model, positioned agent-first with stronger coding and autonomy, and paired that with a global data center rollout and a formal partnership with Nvidia that integrates Nvidia’s “physical AI” software stack—simulation, robotics, and autonomy—into Alibaba’s cloud platform. The market read-through was immediate: Hong Kong shares closed up roughly 9% at a 4‑year high and U.S. ADRs jumped in premarket trading as investors extrapolated higher AI-driven cloud demand, optionality in embodied AI, and a more credible path to international cloud relevance. Management reiterated AI as a core priority alongside commerce and signaled capex could exceed the already-pledged 380 billion yuan over 3 years as infrastructure demand outstrips prior assumptions. The combination of a scaled model roadmap, global capacity, and an Nvidia-aligned software stack is the closest Alibaba has come since 2020 to a cohesive “flywheel” for Cloud and AI.  ￼

On product and platform substance, Qwen3‑Max and the broader Qwen3 family extend Alibaba’s cadence of frequent model upgrades (Qwen 3 in April, Qwen3‑Coder in July) and reinforce a hybrid posture: open‑weight models under Apache‑2.0 to drive developer adoption and API‑only access to the highest‑end checkpoints to preserve monetization and safety control. The company is leaning into reasoning and multi‑modal “omni” variants to compete with DeepSeek’s low-cost reasoning gains and to underpin agentic workflows across commerce, enterprise IT, and mobility. This is not simply a model race; Alibaba pairs models with a platform distribution strategy (Model Studio, Qwen Chat, on‑device MLX support for Apple hardware, and open‑source repos) designed to reduce customer acquisition friction and seed workloads that later graduate to paid cloud services. For investors, this matters because open‑weight availability lowers customer switching costs into Alibaba’s AI stack in markets where its brand is still catching up to AWS/Azure/Google, while API‑only top‑end models protect pricing power where performance differentials drive willingness to pay.  ￼

The Nvidia partnership is more consequential than a headline suggests because it fills a software gap created by hardware uncertainty. Nvidia’s “physical AI” stack—Isaac, Omniverse/RTX‑accelerated simulation, robotics toolchains, and foundation model workflows for embodied systems—has become the reference software environment for developers building robots, autonomous machines, and synthetic data pipelines. By integrating this stack natively into Alibaba Cloud’s Platform for AI, Alibaba can monetize not only LLM training/inference but also simulation compute, digital twins, and AI‑in‑the‑loop testing at scale. In China, embodied intelligence is an explicit policy priority that is driving corporate and state capex into humanoids, logistics robotics, and autonomous systems, which should translate into structurally higher GPU hours, storage, and networking demand on cloud. This aligns Alibaba with a secular upswing in “physical AI” spend while giving it differentiated enterprise tooling relative to domestic rivals that focus more narrowly on chatbots and office copilots. The key nuance: the pact emphasizes software enablement; it does not resolve export‑license risk around top‑end Nvidia silicon in China, implying Alibaba will route sensitive training offshore, multi‑source with domestic accelerators, or emphasize simulation/agents where licensed hardware suffices.  ￼

Global data center expansion is the second pillar and attacks a real constraint: AI customers want low‑latency access to compute, data residency compliance, and credible sovereign controls. Alibaba plans first‑time regions in Brazil, France, and the Netherlands, together with additional capacity in Mexico, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Dubai, and the Philippines. The company frames this as extending a network already spanning ~91 zones across ~29 regions, with AI as the primary design point. This matters for 3 reasons. First, proximity plus data‑localization unlocks regulated workloads and public‑sector bids where Chinese vendors historically struggled. Second, the AI era is shifting cloud unit economics toward higher ARPU workloads with “stickier” consumption curves, so every new compliant region increases the surface area for model/API attach. Third, competition for grid connections and permitting is intensifying in Europe; moving early in France (nuclear‑backed power and a sovereign‑cloud trend), and navigating the Netherlands’ hyperscale constraints, could be a durable advantage if Alibaba secures capacity and sovereignty controls ahead of peers. Risk: Europe’s grid and data‑sovereignty politics are volatile; foreign vendors face additional scrutiny, and the Netherlands’ stringent siting rules increase time‑to‑compute. Execution in these markets will hinge on local partnerships, sovereignty assurances, and price/performance versus incumbents.  ￼

The competitive backdrop inside China remains fierce and is swinging toward reasoning and embodied AI. DeepSeek’s disclosure that it trained R1 at a reported $294,000 on H800s validated a cost‑disruption thesis and forced incumbents to emphasize efficiency and agentic performance, not just raw size. Tencent is simultaneously scaling capex and launching its own reasoning and turbo models while pushing scenario‑based agents and embodied AI toolkits. Alibaba’s response blends model cadence (Qwen series), platform distribution, and the Nvidia alliance to capture embodied‑AI workloads as Beijing accelerates robotics adoption. The strategic implication is that domestic model competition will compress pricing for vanilla LLM APIs; differentiated software stacks (simulation, agents, vertical platforms) are where margin durability will live. For Alibaba equity, success in embodied‑AI workloads could hedge price pressure in consumer chatbot and office‑copilot segments and drive higher compute utilization in Cloud.  ￼

Hardware supply and geopolitics still define the left tail. U.S. export controls removed H100/A100 and later A800/H800 from China, prompting Nvidia’s China‑specific H20/L20/L2 path with uncertain availability and performance. The new Alibaba‑Nvidia pact focuses on software and international regions, which is pragmatic, but near‑term compute elasticity inside China will still depend on domestic accelerators (Huawei Ascend) and Alibaba’s own silicon hedge (Hanguang inference NPUs, Yitian ARM server CPUs). Expect a heterogeneous fleet: offshore high‑end Nvidia for model training, domestic accelerators for inference and simulation, and in‑house chips to manage cost per query in commerce use cases. The investment takeaway is that Alibaba’s AI plan reduces but does not eliminate sanctions risk; valuation should reflect probability‑weighted scenarios where high‑end Nvidia access remains constrained, and ROIC depends on utilization of mixed silicon.  ￼

Financially, the near‑term evidence supports the pivot’s credibility but also highlights capital intensity. In the June quarter, Cloud revenue rose 26% year over year to 33.40 billion yuan, outgrowing the group and driven by AI workloads; the group operating margin was around the mid‑teens. Management previously committed 380 billion yuan over 3 years to AI and is signaling a willingness to spend more as demand materializes. To fund this, Alibaba has layered traditional buybacks with programmatic issuance, including $3.2 billion zero‑coupon converts due 2032 at a 27.5%–32.5% premium, and continued repurchases (~$805 million in the June quarter). The capex ramp will likely lift Cloud growth but may cap consolidated free cash flow conversion until utilization catches up; the convert structure partially mitigates equity dilution via capped calls. From a factor perspective, the stock has re‑rated on AI optionality but remains at a discount to U.S. hyperscalers on P/E and P/S given China risk, governance scars, and commerce margin headwinds. The committee should weigh whether Cloud’s growth mix and AI monetization trajectory can compress that discount over a 12–24 month horizon.  ￼

The commerce backdrop remains a drag and a source of volatility. Domestic e‑commerce is locked in a price war across instant retail and 1‑hour delivery, depressing margins and increasing user acquisition expense. Alibaba has responded with AI‑enabled merchant tools, fee‑structure tweaks, and cross‑platform integration, but the segment still faces competitive pressure from PDD, JD, Douyin, and Meituan. The AI thesis, therefore, must not rely on commerce margin relief; rather, the base case should be that Cloud and AI offset commerce volatility through higher‑growth, higher‑ARPU workloads and that AI improves commerce conversion and ad yield enough to stabilize EBITA. This is achievable but requires disciplined cost control in instant retail subsidies and continued product velocity in Qwen‑powered merchant tooling.  ￼

Internationally, early signs of vertical adoption increase the odds that Alibaba can monetize beyond China. Automotive is a lead indicator: Banma (smart cockpit/autonomy software), in which Alibaba plans to retain ≥30% post‑IPO, is embedding Qwen into OEM assistants, with BMW as a notable reference. Consumer devices (Honor) and edge partners broaden the funnel for inference workloads that ultimately land on Alibaba’s cloud. These are small today versus hyperscaler scale but strategically important because they validate Alibaba’s go‑to‑market in regions where it lacks a long enterprise sales history. The Nvidia partnership should help here; many global robotics and autonomy developers already build against Nvidia’s toolchains, lowering porting friction into Alibaba regions.  ￼

Regulatory and sovereignty risk remains elevated and must be in the underwriting. China’s generative‑AI rules and CAC enforcement increase content filtering and model governance overhead, which can limit exportability of “China‑trained” checkpoints for some Western customers. Outside China, data‑sovereignty requirements in the EU and local scrutiny of Chinese cloud providers raise the bar for certifications, partnerships, and operational “air gaps.” France is relatively attractive given power economics and a maturing sovereign‑cloud regime, whereas the Netherlands’ hyperscale rules, combined with continent‑wide grid constraints, raise execution risk on schedule and capex returns. In the U.S., scrutiny of Chinese cloud/data operators persists. Alibaba’s mitigation playbook—local JVs or managed services models, sovereign controls, and workload partitioning—is necessary but not sufficient; investors should discount EU/US revenue capture until there is evidence of public‑sector or Tier‑1 enterprise wins.  ￼

Investment implications for Alibaba equity are 3‑fold. First, the bull case strengthens: a credible AI product cadence, Nvidia software alignment, and accelerated capacity expansion raise confidence that Cloud can compound at a premium growth rate with rising attach to Qwen APIs, simulation, and agents. If Cloud sustains 20%–30% growth while group commerce stabilizes, blended margins and multiple could re‑rate toward global cloud peers’ discount rather than a deep China conglomerate discount. Catalysts over the next 6–12 months include concrete region launches in Brazil/EU, disclosed AI bookings/backlog, embodied‑AI customer logos, and Banma IPO progress. Second, the bear case is clearer: export control tightening, EU sovereign pushback, or grid/permit delays would strand capex and force greater reliance on domestic accelerators, potentially impairing model parity and Cloud mix. Price wars in commerce could again compress consolidated margins and overshadow Cloud outperformance. Third, the most likely base case is that Alibaba executes a multi‑source compute strategy, keeps Cloud growth in the 20%+ zone with improving unit economics as utilization rises, and uses converts/buybacks to manage dilution; in this case, the stock should continue to close part of the gap to global cloud leaders as the market shifts the narrative from “China platform risk” to “AI infrastructure compounder with China tail risk.”  ￼

Portfolio construction should reflect both upside convexity and policy risk. For directional exposure, a core long in Alibaba sized to tolerate policy shocks is justified if one believes Cloud’s growth path is durable and the AI pipeline converts to revenue. Optionality can be added via call spreads timed around region go‑lives or Qwen milestone releases, funded by writing downside put spreads to reflect the still‑material China risk premium. For relative value, pairing a long Alibaba with a short in a domestic peer more levered to consumer subsidy burn (e.g., instant retail pure‑plays) mitigates commerce price‑war risk and isolates AI/Cloud execution. For cross‑asset hedging, the new 0% 2032 converts offer a way to own upside with downside protection if equity volatility rises into policy events; the cap‑call overlay reduces dilution if the rally extends. Investors with broader AI exposure could complement with Nvidia, but note that the Alibaba‑Nvidia tie‑up is software‑centric and does not resolve silicon licensing, so use Nvidia primarily for its global data center and inference momentum rather than as a pure China proxy.  ￼

What to monitor from here: 1) concrete disclosures on AI bookings, utilization, and attach rates for Qwen APIs and agent/simulation workloads; 2) time‑to‑power and permits in France/Netherlands and whether Alibaba announces sovereign‑cloud partners that satisfy local regulators; 3) evidence of mixed‑silicon parity for inference on Ascend and in‑house NPUs relative to Nvidia in key enterprise benchmarks; 4) embodied‑AI customer wins that validate the Nvidia platform integration (industrial robotics, automotive OEMs, logistics); 5) the competitive response from Tencent, DeepSeek, and Huawei that could reset model economics or shift developer mindshare; and 6) any tightening of U.S. export controls or EU restrictions on Chinese cloud providers that would cap offshore growth. The Apsara slate does not end the debate about China risk, but it materially improves Alibaba’s AI operating leverage and international option value, and it gives the committee a clearer set of KPIs to track for underwrite discipline.  ￼

data.text:
Disparaged political analyst Richard Heydarian is facing backlash again after falsely accusing DDS supporters of sabotaging the September 21 Mendiola protest. On social media, Heydarian claimed: “Mendiola ‘rally’ is looking like DDS sabotage!!! Disown!!! They do NOT represent legitimate anti-corruption forces!!!”

But Heydarian didn’t stop at speculation. In a follow-up post, he definitively declared: “DDS FORCES taking advantage!!! Do NOT ALLOW them to HIJACK the massive PEACEFUL PROTESTS!!!”—crossing the line from conjecture into outright falsehood.

That claim has since been debunked. The Manila Police District later confirmed that those arrested were members of Akbayan Partylist, ACT Teachers, and Gabriela. MPD spokesperson P/Maj. Philip Ines stated: “Kanina po nandito po yung Akbayan Partylist, yung ACT Teachers at yung Gabriela. Base po sa nakuha nating impormasyon, may mga miyembro po sila doon sa mga nahuli natin.” He added that seven lawyers had already visited the detainees to check their condition.

Gabriela Women’s Party backed this up in a statement, saying that Rep. Sarah Elago, Kabataan Rep. Renee Co, and ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio went to the precinct to check on the detainees. They also called for the release of minors and PWDs, demanding that their Miranda rights be respected.

The violence that erupted, however, went far beyond simple dispersals. DILG Secretary Jonvic Remulla alleged that some participants were recruited for as much as ₱3,000 each, with reports of children as young as 11 years old being used. He revealed chilling instructions given to them: “Kung kaya [niyong] umabot ng Palasyo, sunugin niyo.”

That context makes the death of 15-year-old Justine Serbio Ignacio even more tragic. Ignacio was stabbed along Recto Avenue after reportedly joining the chaos. The suspect, a 52-year-old watch technician, claimed he acted in defense of his property after minors tried to damage motorbikes. He later surrendered and now faces charges.

Manila Mayor Isko Moreno confirmed that more than 100 police officers were injured and millions of pesos in property were destroyed. He denied rumors of fatalities during the riot itself but reminded the public that violence only breeds more violence. Investigators are now probing two suspected financiers allegedly tied to a political group.

Heydarian’s false claim did more than just miss the mark—it caused real damage. By wrongly blaming DDS supporters, he smeared an entire group without evidence and inflamed an already volatile situation. His statement also distracted the public from the actual groups confirmed by police to be involved, shifting attention away from the serious issues of recruitment, exploitation of minors, and violent instructions that fueled the chaos. Worse, by pointing fingers at the wrong people, his misinformation risked shielding the true financiers and organizers from accountability. And in the middle of all this, a 15-year-old boy lost his life—making Heydarian’s reckless words not just misleading, but a cruel distortion that trivialized tragedy and muddied the search for justice.

Adding to the irony, Heydarian has historically aligned himself with the politics very groups that police later identified as being involved in or supportive of the Mendiola chaos. For him to attack DDS while shielding allies only underscored the double standards and opportunism behind his narrative.

And this was not an isolated mistake—it is part of a pattern. He once compared Mindanao’s Human Development Index to Sub-Saharan Africa, a statement widely condemned as demeaning, with several LGUs even declaring him persona non grata.

He also twisted Senator Ping Lacson’s warning on flood-control spending, telling readers in his Inquirer column that the country had “lost close to ₱1 trillion” under Duterte. 

In truth, Lacson never said money was “lost”—he said ₱1.9 trillion was appropriated from 2011 to 2025, with ₱1 trillion of that allocated in ...

data.text:
KIKO TO COA: PROBE ALL AUDITORS INVOLVED IN FLOOD CONTROL PROJECTS

Senator Kiko Pangilinan on Wednesday, September 24, urged the Commission on Audit (COA) to launch a comprehensive probe into all auditors involved in the planning, approval, and execution of flood mitigation programs amid the multi-billion peso corruption scandal.

The call came after former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Bulacan district engineer Henry Alcantara tagged COA Commissioner Mario Lipana for allegedly requesting a list of flood control projects in his district to facilitate ₱1.4 billion worth of budget insertions.

At a House COA hearing on September 11, it was revealed that Lipana's wife, Marilou, president and general manager of Olympus Mining and Builders Group Philippines Corporation, had secured several DPWH flood control contracts totaling ₱326 million.

"Saan ka naman nakakita na COA commissioner ka tapos maglalako ka ng listahan ng flood control projects? Tapos malalaman natin na ang kanyang misis pala ay isang contractor ng DPWH na nakatanggap ng daan-daang milyong halaga na kontrata?" Pangilinan said.

The senator stressed the need for transparency and accountability, citing reports of irregular procurement, substandard implementation, and possible collusion between government officials and private contractors.

"Bawat pisong ninakaw mula sa mga proyektong ito ay pagtataksil sa taong bayan, lalong lalo na yung mga buhay, bahay, at pangkabuhayan na nalalagay sa panganib tuwing may bagyo, ulan, at baha," he added.

His remarks came days after tens of thousands joined the "Trillion Peso March" to denounce the scandal, which allegedly involves top government officials and several private firms.

MAYOR JOY 🤝 RAMON ANG

Magtutulungan sina Mayor Joy Belmonte at San Miguel Corporation Chairman and CEO Ramon S. Ang upang tugunan ang pagbabahang nararanasan sa Lungsod Quezon.

Tinalakay sa pulong ang planong pagtatayo ng Detention Basin sa G. Araneta Avenue, paglalagay ng stormwater storage tunnel system, at dredging works sa creeks at waterways sa QC.

Kasama ng Alkalde sa meeting sina District 1 Action Officer Ollie Belmonte at City Engineer Atty. Dale Perral.
